prompt: What does predicting the mean give as a regression baseline?
title: Regression Baseline: Predicting the Mean
body:
When evaluating a regression model, we need a simple benchmark to beat. The simplest naive approach is predicting the mean value of the targets for every single input sample.

Notice in the plot how the horizontal line sits right through the middle of the scatter points.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"A constant mean baseline","caption":"Illustrative values; the horizontal mean line minimizes squared error.","kind":"coordinate-plot","x":{"label":"Sample","min":1,"max":8},"y":{"label":"Target","min":20,"max":50},"series":[{"label":"Targets","kind":"scatter","points":[{"x":1,"y":25},{"x":2,"y":45},{"x":3,"y":39},{"x":4,"y":42},{"x":5,"y":35},{"x":6,"y":23},{"x":7,"y":43},{"x":8,"y":32}]}],"annotations":[{"kind":"reference-line","label":"Mean prediction $\\bar{y} = 35.5$","axis":"y","value":35.5}]}}
```

This constant prediction serves as our baseline model. It yields total squared error equal to the variance of the data multiplied by the sample size, forming the foundation of $R^2$ scoring.

diagrams.caption: Illustrative values; the horizontal mean line minimizes squared error.

prompt: What does predicting the mean give as a regression baseline?
title: Regression baseline with mean prediction
body:
Predicting the mean target value provides a simple reference model called a baseline. This constant prediction minimizes squared error without using any features.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Constant mean baseline","caption":"Illustrative values showing targets and the mean prediction line.","kind":"coordinate-plot","x":{"label":"Sample index","min":0,"max":8},"y":{"label":"Target value","min":0,"max":60},"series":[{"label":"Targets","kind":"scatter","points":[{"x":1,"y":31},{"x":2,"y":32},{"x":3,"y":45},{"x":4,"y":51},{"x":5,"y":40},{"x":6,"y":29},{"x":7,"y":15},{"x":8,"y":19}]}],"annotations":[{"kind":"reference-line","label":"Mean $32.75$","axis":"y","value":32.75}]}}
```

To compute this baseline, sum the target values and divide by the count of samples. For our illustrative case, the targets are $31$, $32$, $45$, $51$, $40$, $29$, $15$, and $19$.

Their sum is $262$, yielding a mean of $32.75$.

Any candidate regression model must beat this constant prediction to be useful. If a sophisticated algorithm yields higher error than this simple average, it fails to capture meaningful patterns.

body:
When building a regression model, we often start with a simple baseline to judge if our features actually help. A common choice is predicting the constant mean of the target values for every single input sample.

Look for the horizontal reference line in the plot above, which sits right at the average value of the scatter points.


title: Predicting the Mean as a Regression Baseline
body:
When evaluating a regression model, comparing its error to a naive benchmark helps judge its actual utility.

Using the average of the target values as a constant prediction provides this simple reference point, known as the mean baseline.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"A constant mean baseline","caption":"Illustrative values; the geometry shows the constant mean prediction against targets.","kind":"coordinate-plot","x":{"label":"Sample","min":0,"max":9},"y":{"label":"Target","min":0,"max":70},"series":[{"label":"Targets","kind":"scatter","points":[{"x":1,"y":53},{"x":2,"y":30},{"x":3,"y":13},{"x":4,"y":44},{"x":5,"y":31},{"x":6,"y":11},{"x":7,"y":58},{"x":8,"y":22}]}],"annotations":[{"kind":"reference-line","label":"Mean prediction of 32.75","axis":"y","value":32.75}]}}
```

For any input, this baseline always guesses the arithmetic mean of all target values in the dataset.

Looking at the plot, notice how the horizontal line represents this single constant value across all samples regardless of their input features.

Minimizing squared error dictates that the mean is precisely the optimal constant predictor for a set of values.

prompt: What does predicting the mean give as a regression baseline?
title: Predicting the Mean as a Regression Baseline
body:
When evaluating a regression model, predicting the mean provides a simple constant baseline. For any input, this baseline guesses the average value of the target variable from the training set.

It serves as a sanity check for more complex models.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"A constant mean baseline","caption":"Illustrative values; targets plotted against a constant mean prediction.","kind":"coordinate-plot","x":{"label":"Sample","min":0,"max":6},"y":{"label":"Target","min":0,"max":60},"series":[{"label":"Targets","kind":"scatter","points":[{"x":1,"y":43},{"x":2,"y":45},{"x":3,"y":17},{"x":4,"y":56},{"x":5,"y":10}]}],"annotations":[{"kind":"reference-line","label":"Mean prediction of 34.2","axis":"y","value":34.2}]}}
```

The plot shows the targets and the constant mean prediction line. The squared errors between the targets and this mean line sum to the total variance of the data.

If a machine learning model cannot beat this total error, it has learned nothing useful.

title: Confusion matrix with exact counts
body:
A confusion matrix tabulates how many items a classifier got right or wrong. The rows list the true class, the columns the predicted class.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Confusion matrix with exact counts","caption":"Heatmap shows counts; darker color = higher count","kind":"heatmap","rowLabel":"Actual","columnLabel":"Predicted","columns":["Negative","Positive"],"rows":[{"label":"Negative","cells":[46,19]},{"label":"Positive","cells":[11,35]}],"range":{"min":11,"max":46},"highlights":[{"row":1,"column":1}]}}
```

In this example the true‑negative count (TN) is 46, false‑positive (FP) 19, false‑negative (FN) 11, and true‑positive (TP) 35. These exact numbers let us compute performance metrics.

Precision = $\frac{TP}{TP+FP}=\frac{35}{35+19}=0.65$, recall = $\frac{TP}{TP+FN}=\frac{35}{35+11}=0.76$, and specificity = $\frac{TN}{TN+FP}=\frac{46}{46+19}=0.71$.

The heatmap’s colour intensity reflects each count: the darkest cell (TN) shows the highest value, while the lightest (FN) shows the lowest.

diagrams.caption: Heatmap shows counts; darker color = higher count

prompt: Explain a confusion matrix with exact counts.
title: Confusion Matrix Counts
body:
A confusion matrix tracks classification performance by counting correct and incorrect predictions against true labels.

Suppose we evaluate a model on 123 samples using our starting counts 29, 10, 27, 19, 36, 5, 14, and 58.

Look for the split between classes in the heatmap below, where rows represent actual outcomes and columns show model predictions.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Actual and predicted classes","caption":"The highlighted cell shows actual positives predicted negative.","kind":"heatmap","rowLabel":"Actual","columnLabel":"Predicted","columns":["Negative","Positive"],"rows":[{"label":"Negative","cells":[58,10]},{"label":"Positive","cells":[19,36]}],"range":{"min":10,"max":58},"highlights":[{"row":1,"column":0}]}}
```

The matrix organizes outcomes into true negatives, false positives, false negatives, and true positives.

Here we find 58 true negatives and 36 true positives along the diagonal, alongside 10 false positives and 19 false negatives off the diagonal.

body:
A confusion matrix displays the performance of a classification model by comparing actual labels against predicted outcomes across classes.

Each cell tallies instances where the model succeeds or makes specific types of errors during evaluation.

Look for the counts distributed across the four outcomes in the heatmap below, which total 129 observations in this illustrative case.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Actual and predicted classes","caption":"The highlighted cell shows actual positives predicted as negative.","kind":"heatmap","rowLabel":"Actual","columnLabel":"Predicted","columns":["Negative","Positive"],"rows":[{"label":"Negative","cells":[26,15]},{"label":"Positive","cells":[42,46]}],"range":{"min":15,"max":46},"highlights":[{"row":1,"column":0}]}}
```

The top-left cell shows 26 true negatives, while the bottom-right cell shows 46 true positives correctly identified by the system.

Errors appear off-diagonal, such as the 42 false negatives highlighted where positive instances were missed.

title: How “sat” attends to the sentence
body:
In a self-attention mechanism, words compute relevance scores against every other word in the sequence.

When the query word sat evaluates the sentence the cat sat on the mat, it assigns a specific weight to each target token.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Attention weights from “sat”","caption":"Thicker arrows carry more weight. In this example, the six weights from “sat” sum to 1.00.","kind":"token-links","source":["the","cat","sat","on","the","mat"],"target":["the","cat","sat","on","the","mat"],"queries":[{"index":2,"weights":[0.1,0.4,0.2,0.1,0.05,0.15]}],"normalized":true}}
```

The diagram shows these attention weights originating from the query token sat. Notice how cat receives the largest weight of 0.40, because the subject directly performs the action.

All six weights sum to one, ensuring a proper probability distribution over the input sequence.

Auxiliary words like on receive lower scores since they provide weaker contextual links to the verb than the subject or object.
